title: AI - MCP for Dummies
tagline: The universal connector for AI, no custom hacks needed.
description: A 60-card guided run through the core ideas that actually matter.

modules.title: What MCP Really Is
modules.summary: The core mental model behind the Model Context Protocol.

cards.content: MCP stands for Model Context Protocol: an open-source standard that lets AI apps connect securely to external data, tools, and systems.
Think of MCP as USB-C for AI. One universal plug that works with any data source or tool instead of building custom adapters every time.
Anthropic introduced MCP in November 2024 to replace fragmented integrations with a single, standardized protocol.
MCP enables LLMs like Claude or ChatGPT to fetch live data, run tools, and perform actions without leaving their training cutoff behind.
It is built on JSON-RPC 2.0, making it simple, lightweight, and easy for developers to implement.
MCP is two-way: AI can request context from servers and servers can push updates or ask for human approval.
The protocol turns static AI models into dynamic agents that can read files, query databases, or trigger workflows.
Adoption is already widespread: OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Cursor, VS Code, and many IDEs support MCP out of the box.
MCP is open source and vendor-neutral. Anyone can build servers or clients without permission.
If you remember one thing: MCP is less a new AI model and more a universal socket that plugs any AI into the real world.

modules.title: Why MCP Matters
modules.summary: The problem it solves and the gap it fills.

cards.content: Before MCP, every AI tool needed custom code to talk to each database, API, or file system. That was slow and error-prone.
LLMs are stuck with outdated training data. MCP gives them live, real-time context on demand.
Custom integrations break easily when systems change. MCP provides one stable interface that everyone can rely on.
Agentic AI needs to act, not just chat. MCP supplies the standardized way for models to call tools and get results.
Developers waste weeks building one-off connectors. MCP lets them build once and reuse everywhere.
Security and permissions are built in from day one. MCP servers control exactly what the AI can see or do.
Human-in-the-loop is native: servers can pause and ask a person for approval before sensitive actions.
MCP reduces hallucinations by grounding AI answers in fresh, verified external data.
It accelerates the shift from chatbots to autonomous agents that can actually get work done.
The big idea: MCP is the missing standard that finally makes AI as plug-and-play as the rest of the internet.

modules.title: MCP Architecture
modules.summary: The client-server model that powers everything.

cards.content: MCP uses a simple client-server architecture. The AI host runs an MCP client; external systems run MCP servers.
Clients are inside the AI app (Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, etc.). They discover and talk to any available MCP server.
Servers expose three things: resources (files/data), tools (functions the AI can call), and prompts (pre-written workflows).
Communication happens over HTTP, SSE, or WebSockets. Everything is JSON-RPC messages.
Servers declare their capabilities upfront so the AI knows exactly what it can ask for.
Sessions are stateful when needed, letting the AI maintain context across multiple tool calls.
Discovery is automatic. Clients scan for local or remote MCP servers without manual configuration.
Permissions are granular: each server decides what the AI can read, write, or execute.
The design is intentionally lightweight so even small tools or personal scripts can become MCP servers.
This clean separation means AI models stay focused on reasoning while the heavy lifting happens outside.

modules.title: Building MCP Servers
modules.summary: How to expose your data and tools to AI.

cards.content: Anyone can write an MCP server in any language. Official SDKs exist for Python, Java, TypeScript, and more.
A server simply implements a few RPC methods: list resources, read files, call tools, etc.
You can wrap existing APIs, databases, or local folders and turn them into secure MCP endpoints.
Reference implementations from Anthropic make it easy to start with Google Drive, Notion, GitHub, or Slack.
Servers can be local (on your laptop) or remote (cloud-hosted) and still work the same way.
Authentication uses standard OAuth or API keys. The AI never sees your raw credentials.
Rate limiting, logging, and audit trails are built into every server for enterprise safety.
You can expose entire workflows as reusable prompts that the AI can trigger with one call.
Once published, your server works instantly with every MCP-compatible AI app on the market.
Building servers is the fastest way to give AI superpowers tailored exactly to your data and processes.

modules.title: Using MCP with AI Models
modules.summary: How agents actually call tools and get context.

cards.content: When an AI needs information, it sends an MCP request to the connected server instead of guessing.
The model decides which tool or resource to use based on the server’s declared capabilities.
Responses come back as structured data that the model can reason over in the same conversation.
Chain-of-thought works naturally: the AI can call multiple tools in sequence to complete complex tasks.
Human approval flows are automatic. The server can pause and show a confirmation dialog.
Context windows stay manageable because only the needed data is pulled in on demand.
Popular clients (Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code Copilot) already surface MCP servers in their UI.
No prompt engineering tricks required. The model just asks the server and gets clean, verified answers.
You can switch AI models or hosts without rewriting any connectors. The protocol stays the same.
The result is AI that feels truly connected to your world instead of living in its own bubble.

modules.title: Limits, Security, and the Road Ahead
modules.summary: Where the cracks show and what comes next.

cards.content: MCP inherits the security model of whatever servers you connect. A badly written server can expose data.
Not every AI host supports MCP yet, though adoption is growing extremely fast.
Latency can add up when the AI makes many sequential tool calls across slow networks.
Servers still need maintenance. Updates to underlying APIs can break even standardized connectors.
Overly permissive servers risk giving AI too much power. Always follow least-privilege rules.
Privacy-conscious users can run everything locally with self-hosted MCP servers.
The ecosystem is young. Best practices for discovery, versioning, and error handling are still evolving.
Future versions will add richer streaming, multi-agent coordination, and built-in memory layers.
MCP is becoming the foundation for the next wave of truly agentic AI that can act across all your tools.
The smartest way to use MCP is this: treat it as leverage that keeps humans in control while giving AI the context it needs to shine.
